headline: High: shared MCP and broad network/file access create dangerous default pathways for prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent ingests MCP/stdin-stdout and can run browsers/subprocesses; OpenHands also uses MCP and browser/tool loops. That creates a plausible content bridge where one agent’s outputs can be treated as instructions by the other, especially through shared MCP servers or copied artifacts. No direct shared channel is documented, so I choose medium rather than low because the pathway exists in default tool-heavy setups.
conditions: IF both agents connect to the same MCP server or relay, injected instructions can traverse between them.
IF OpenHands forwards LightAgent-generated text into a tool prompt, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Use separate MCP servers per agent.
Strip instructions from any text passed between agents.
Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent messages.
Disable browser/tool execution on untrusted content paths.
requires-engineering: enforce allowlisted message schemas between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches user conversations, long-term memory, trace data, tool calls/results, and secrets; OpenHands reads mounted files and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive content from LightAgent can be exposed to OpenHands and then sent onward by its networked runtime. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default multi-agent deployments, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents share a mounted volume or workspace, OpenHands can read LightAgent artifacts.
IF LightAgent writes secrets or trace data into shared files, OpenHands can exfiltrate them over network egress.
mitigations: Keep separate workspaces and mounts.
Store secrets only in per-agent secret stores.
Rotate any API keys used by LightAgent.
Audit shared directories for traces and logs.
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls and redaction before handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem, modify git state, install packages, and execute shell commands; LightAgent can spawn subprocesses and use MCP, with multiple instances supported. If both operate on the same repo or runtime volume, concurrent writes and git mutations can corrupt state or overwrite each other. Because the default OpenHands runtime is writable and LightAgent has active tool execution, high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or mounted volume, write conflicts can occur.
IF both modify git state without an external lock, commits or working trees can be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable package installs in one agent during shared runs.
Use read-only mounts for the non-authoring agent.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent produces tool calls/results, workflow state, and provenance metadata, while OpenHands runs an agent loop that can act on shell/browser/editor outputs. If OpenHands treats LightAgent output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into real actions such as file edits or commits. The downstream action authority in OpenHands makes this a high-severity default risk.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes LightAgent output without verification, incorrect facts can propagate into actions.
IF LightAgent emits malformed provenance metadata, OpenHands may act on it as if validated.
mitigations: Require human review before actions.
Add a verification step between agents.
Pass only structured, schema-validated outputs.
Log and diff proposed changes before execution.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating for downstream actions.

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent handles secrets and long-term memory, while OpenHands runs in a Docker runtime with mounted files and model-provider keys. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different retention and storage surfaces for sensitive data classes. That creates a compliance gap risk around logging, retention, and subject-rights handling, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into LightAgent memory or OpenHands-mounted files, retention obligations may diverge.
IF logs from either agent are retained longer than policy allows, deletion/export requests can fail.
mitigations: Classify data before use.
Disable or shorten logs for sensitive runs.
Keep regulated data out of shared mounts.
Document retention for each agent separately.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across the pair.
